OBSERVE · COMPARE · UNDERSTAND

Three ways to explore atomic structure

1. Build an electron configuration

Place electrons one at a time. Read orbital boxes, compare shell totals, and see Aufbau, Hund’s rule and Pauli pairing in action. The filling lesson currently covers hydrogen to calcium.

Open the filling animation →

2. See the shape of an orbital

Open the viewer and choose hydrogen orbitals. Rotate the probability cloud to see lobes and nodes from different angles. Quantum numbers describe the state; the point cloud shows its spatial distribution.

Open the 3D viewer →

3. Explore a complete atom

In the viewer, choose Element Explorer. Compare elements and use shell dissection to inspect the occupied subshells. This wider atom model complements the introductory filling lesson.

Explore elements →

Shell, subshell or orbital?

TermMeaningElectron capacity
ShellA principal level identified by n, such as n = 2.At most 2n²
SubshellA family within a shell: s, p, d or f.2, 6, 10 or 14
OrbitalOne spatial state within a subshell; shown as one box.At most 2, with opposite spins

Shells do not simply fill one after another. For example, 4s begins before 3d. Use calcium to see the difference between a shell’s capacity and its actual occupancy.

Questions about atoms and electrons

Are the dots individual electrons?

No. Each dot is a sampled possible position. Together they show the spatial probability distribution, rather than a path around the nucleus.

What do the arrows in an orbital diagram mean?

They label electron spin states. Two arrows in the same box must have opposite directions; equal-energy orbitals fill singly before electrons pair.

Is the filling animation an exact atom simulation?

It is a teaching diagram with schematic cloud shapes. The 3D atom viewer uses the project’s radial models and sampling calculations; the guides explain their construction.
